A candle on a table should meet your eye, not sit above it.

The flame belongs below the eyeline of the people seated, or above their heads. Anywhere in between it blinds, and two guests facing each other stop looking at each other. Below means a candlestick of twenty centimetres, not forty.

They are lit when the first guest walks into the room. Never before.

Twelve at a table that does not stand still.

Everything on a boat is laid for movement: nothing round, nothing tall, glasses with a low centre, cloth weighted at the corners rather than clipped. The galley is four square metres, so the cooking happens ashore and only the finishing happens here.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number one.

The bloom on a grape is not dust, and it does not wash off.

That pale film on the skin is wild yeast. It sits there on its own and it is what ferments the fruit. A bunch that arrives shining is a bunch that has already been washed, which means it is already a few days old.

So it comes into the kitchen like this, and it goes onto the table like this.

A cigar outlasts any dessert.

Forty minutes, and forty minutes in which nobody stands up: whoever opens one has decided to stay. It needs air that moves and an amaro that can carry smoke, and it is not the moment for coffee.

The kitchen has already been taken apart. Nobody in the other room notices.

A cloister is a room with no roof and four walls of shade, which is why it works in September and stops working in the middle of October.

Fifty covers fit down the centre. The paving takes a trolley, the arcade takes the service line, and the sky decides everything else.

A ripe fig tells you by weeping.

When it is ready it loses a bead of syrup at the eye and the skin splits on its own. Pick it the day before and neither happens; the day after, you find it on the ground. The window is about forty-eight hours.

Which is why in September figs are bought in the morning and served the same evening.

The same cloister, eight hours later.

Thirty covers down the middle, and every plate came through the arcade carried, because nothing rolls on paving laid in the fifteenth century. The kitchen is two rooms away and nobody at this table will ever see it.

It is not a venue. It opens for one evening, and then it closes again.

Nobody pours for a toast standing up.

The glasses are filled before anyone is asked to raise one, because twenty people lifting glasses while somebody is still moving behind them is how a jacket gets ruined. Two of us go round the outside, never between the chairs, and it takes under a minute.

Then everybody is holding something at the same time, which is all a toast really is.

Teak is the reason nobody wears heels on this deck.

It is laid to be walked on wet and scrubbed with salt water, and it marks under anything with a point. Trolleys do not come aboard: every plate arrives carried, up a passerelle with a handrail on one side only.

A porcino is judged by the stem, not by the cap.

If the stem gives under your thumb the mushroom is gone, and the grub only shows when you open it. Which is why they are bought whole and opened one by one, and why at least one in ten is thrown away. The price already accounts for that.

The good ones never arrive all at once.

A courtyard behind a town palazzo is the only quiet square metre in the middle of a city.

The gate is the whole problem. Everything that goes in goes through it, and the paving is old enough that the wheels have to be large ones: small castors drop into the joints and stop dead.

A table lit only by candles is lit from below.

It flatters everything on it and nothing above it, so whatever matters sits low and the centre stays under fifteen centimetres. Tall arrangements are how a room ends up dark with a bright stripe down the middle of it.

The one thing you never do is add a lamp to fix it.

The same courtyard, after sunset.

Twenty-four covers, and all the light is on the table: the walls climb eight metres and nothing reaches above four. It is the easiest room in the dossier to light, and the one where you watch the forecast until the last afternoon.

A private courtyard in the centre of a city is not for hire. You ask for it.

It is not a promise about style. It is the size of the company, and it is the reason you can check it.

What goes wrong at an important dinner is almost never the cooking. It is being the fourth event of that Saturday.

A terrace has one advantage and one problem, and they are the same thing.

Nothing above it. Which means the light is right until it is not, and the whole evening is built around a single hour: drinks outside, dinner inside, and a changeover rehearsed because it has to happen in the time it takes to serve one round.

White truffle is bought by weight, and it is lost by weight.

From the moment it comes out of the ground it loses weight every day, and what leaves is water: the truffle weighed on Monday is not there on Saturday. It is kept at four degrees wrapped in paper, and the paper is changed daily.

It is never cooked. It goes on at the last second, and the plate underneath has to be hot.

A frescoed hall comes with one rule that is not negotiable: nothing touches the walls.

Which sounds simple until you put fifty covers in a room whose perimeter is out of bounds. The table goes down the centre, the service line runs behind the chairs, and the field kitchen goes two rooms away.

Dessert in a glass is not laziness. It is arithmetic.

Fifty plated desserts take twenty minutes to assemble and six minutes to serve, which does not work. In a glass they are made in the morning, they sit in the fridge, and they come out together. By that hour the kitchen is already half dismantled, and this is the only way to do it without anybody noticing.

The spoon is long. That part is not an aesthetic choice.

The same hall, and nothing is touching the walls.

Fifty covers down the centre, the service line behind the chairs, the field kitchen two rooms away. That is the entire plan, and it is dictated by the frescoes rather than by us. No chandelier is switched on: the flames sit lower than the paintings, so the room reads and the ceiling goes dark.

Houses like this say yes to about one evening a season.

New oil is judged in the throat, not on the tongue.

The catch that arrives two seconds later is polyphenol, and if it is not there the oil is either old or it has been heated. It does not last: by March that oil is a different oil.

You buy it in November and you do not wait.

At anchor there is no second run.

Whatever was forgotten stays forgotten, so the list is checked twice on the quay and once more before the lines come off. Water is the limit rather than power: a boat carries what it carries, and the washing up is done ashore the next morning.

An amaro is chosen by the hour, not by what was eaten.

Before midnight the ones with more herb and less sugar; after midnight the other way round. That is why there are six on the trolley and not twenty, and why none of the six is poured at the table.

By then the kitchen has already gone back out through the door it came in.

An oyster is served cold, not iced.

It rests on the ice, never in it: if meltwater gets into the shell it carries off the liquor, which is the part you are paying for. And it is opened to order, because an oyster opened half an hour early has already lost twice.

Six minutes from the bench to the table. Beyond that, the menu changes.

A refectory was designed for exactly this, and then stopped being used for it.

One long wall of fresco, a stone floor that takes anything, and acoustics built for a single voice reading aloud, which means fifty people talking sound like two hundred. Cloth on the table and something soft at both ends, or the room wins.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number eight.

The second hour is the one that decides the evening.

By then the food is doing less work than the room: how loud it is, how far apart people are sitting, whether the light has come down. A table held at the same brightness from eight to midnight empties by eleven.

We take the light down twice. Nobody has ever mentioned it.

The same refectory, and the problem is not the table. It is the echo.

A hall built so that a single voice would carry to the far end gives forty people back as two hundred. Fabric goes where it cannot be seen, under the cloth and at both ends, and the light comes down, because people speak more quietly in a darker room. It works, and nobody understands why.

By day the visitors walk through it. In the evening it belongs to whoever asked for it.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number eight, at night.

The door is the last thing we open.

Two hours before this the room was full of crates and four of us moving fast. By the time it opens there is nothing in here that belongs to us except the table, and the passage outside has been swept.

Nobody sees the two hours. That is the job.

At six in the morning Florence is a city of deliveries.

The trolley is on the paving because the van does not come in: inside the walls you unload at the gate and push, and the distance between the gate and the door decides how many times you go back and forth. Fifty covers is between four and six runs.

By seven the street belongs to the people who live on it again.

Dinner ends when somebody stands up, not when dessert is finished.

Which is why the next room has been ready for an hour: armchairs already grouped in fours, light two thirds lower than the dining room, and nothing to eat. Anyone who moves has to find a seat within three paces, or they go back to the table and the evening sits down again.

The move is never announced. A door is opened.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. Private dinners in Tuscany, from the first glass to the swept floor.

The last room we show is the one we would have started with.

Five tall windows down one side, a floor that takes any weight, and enough distance from the entrance that a hundred people can arrive before the room knows it. It has no kitchen either. None of them do.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number nine.

Six twenty in the morning, and nothing has been cooked yet.

Everything you see was carried in. Induction, 32 kW, through a door 1.10 m wide, which is the number that decides what is on the menu more often than the menu does.

Two hours to build. Gone by morning, and the floor from 1490 unmarked.

The same room, sixty covers, one table.

Sixty at a single table is a decision and not a constraint: two tables of thirty are easier to serve, and they make two parties instead of one. So the table runs the length of the room, the brigade works from both ends inward, and the last plate goes down within four minutes of the first.

There is no kitchen in this building. There never was.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number nine, at night.

The door decides the menu more often than the menu does.

A loggia is half a room, and the missing half decides everything.

No wall on the garden side means no power on that side either, so the service line runs along the wall behind and the field kitchen goes out of sight in the courtyard. Forty covers along the length, one row, never two.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number ten.

A board is not a large plate.

It is composed to be taken apart: everything has to be lifted without moving anything else, and the last person to arrive has to find it still legible. So it is built in sectors rather than in a heap, and the cheeses sit on the opposite side from where the wine is poured.

After ten minutes it becomes a different object. That one has to stand up too.

A room built to hold wine, not people. Brick vaults, two empty vats, and a stone channel in the floor that still runs the right way.

No kitchen, no power beyond one bare bulb, and a door that takes the trolley only if you take the wheels off first.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number eleven.

Three glasses per place, and two of them will not be used.

They go down anyway, because the third one is for whatever gets opened after the second course, and a table you have to add to halfway through has already lost the evening.

The napkin is bordeaux. That part is not practical.

The same vat room, between the two vats.

Twenty covers in a room built for wine and not for people: brick vaults, a drainage channel in the floor and one bare bulb. Everything you can see arrived from outside, and the door takes the trolley only if you take the wheels off first.

Rooms like this are on nobody's price list.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number eleven, at night.

Halfway through, a table stops looking laid and starts looking used.

This is the state we work towards rather than away from: bread broken where somebody reached for it, glasses at different levels, a napkin left on a chair. A table that still looks photographed at ten o'clock is a table where nobody has relaxed.

We clear the plates. We leave the rest alone.

A villa with a kitchen is still a villa without a kitchen.

The one that is there is domestic: two burners, one oven, one sink, and a fridge that runs at eight degrees instead of four. It is somewhere to set down and somewhere to wash, not somewhere to cook for fifty. The field kitchen comes anyway, and this room becomes the place where the plates go out.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number twelve.

A larder that travels is counted in crates, not in shelves.

The night before it is all inside, weighed, and no crate goes over twenty-five kilos, because one person has to carry it up a staircase with no lift. That constraint is what decides how many jars, and how much glass.

Glass always loses. It gets decanted.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. We build a full kitchen where there is none, and take it out again the same night.

A cellar is the only room in the dossier that does not change temperature.

It sits between twelve and fourteen degrees all year, which is perfect for the wine and wrong for everything else: the plates are heated elsewhere and arrive covered, and the bread is cut at the last minute because down here it dries in twenty minutes.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number thirteen.

Meat rests almost as long as it cooked.

Straight from the fire to the board and the liquid ends up on the table instead of in the plate. Twenty minutes somewhere warm does not cool it down: it makes it carvable. The plate underneath, on the other hand, has to be hot enough to hurt.

It is the only moment in the service when the right thing to do is wait.

The same cellar, at twelve degrees all year round.

Perfect for the wine and wrong for everything else. The plates are heated two rooms away and carried covered, and the bread is cut at the last minute because down here it dries in twenty minutes. The vault takes the sound and gives nothing back, so eighteen people at one table sound like eight.

Nobody advertises a room like this. You have to know that it exists.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number thirteen, at night.

Fifty covers, and the last thing to go down is the water.

The table is built from the centre outwards, because the centre is the only line that has to be straight and everything else is measured off it. Nine candlesticks, none of them lit, because a candle lit before the guests arrive is a candle half gone by the second course.

The room stays like this for about forty minutes. Then it is never this quiet again.

The dossier asks the same seven questions of every place. Who allows an outside brigade, where the field kitchen goes, how much power is on site, how the vans get in, how late we can stay, who signs the permit, what it costs.

The answers are the reason we can say yes quickly.

This is the part nobody photographs.

The room empties over about twenty minutes and stays exactly as it was left. Then two of us take it apart: everything that came in goes back out the same night, through the same door, and the floor is swept before anybody locks up.
